newsitem.title: FRANCE: Vietnam's "Playboy Emperor" buried in Paris.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam's "Playboy Emperor" buried in Paris.

text.p: Vietnam's last monarch, "Playboy Emperor" Bao Dai, was buried in Paris on Wednesday after a funeral attended by veterans of France's Indochina War and ignored by the Communist government in Hanoi.

French President Jacques Chirac sent a senior aide but the Socialist government was not represented at the service for the former puppet ruler, who died in Paris last week aged 83 after four decades in exile.

French Indochina veterans, responding to an appeal by the far-right National Front, turned up to serve as pallbearers and carry the French flag during the sombre funeral in the chic 16th arrondissement of Paris.
There were no Vietnamese flags and Hanoi, which says Bao Dai failed history by refusing to help build a communist state with Ho Chi Minh after World War Two, was not represented.
Bao Dai, who was born Nguyen Vinh Thuy in 1913, was crowned emperor at the age of 13 and assumed his royal duties at Hue, the Imperial City, six years later in 1932.
After failing to convince Paris to introduce reforms, he spent most of his time in France and then, back in Vietnam, collaborated with the wartime Japanese occupiers.

Bao Dai, known for his jetsetting lifestyle, abdicated in favour of the communist Viet Minh in 1945 and was named "Citizen Prince Nguyen Vinh Thuy" by Ho, but soon left his advisory post for a life of leisure in Hong Kong.
He returned in 1949 and was reinstalled by the French as monarch, but let his pro-French aides run the government.
Following Ho Chi Minh's victory at Dien Bien Phu in 1954 and France's withdrawal from Vietnam, Bao Dai left for exile in southern France and played no further political role in his country's affairs.
About 800 people, including his French-born widow Princess Monique Vinh Tuy, French aristocrats and former royalist Vietnamese officers, attended the funeral mass.

In his eulogy, Roger Holeindre, leader of an Indochina veterans association close to the National Front, praised Bao Dai as a dedicated anti-communist who did not see France's struggle against the Viet Minh as a colonial war.
When he died last Thursday, the French government hailed Bao Dai as a "true friend of our country."
